summary: This unit teaches you to plan, build, check and protect complex spreadsheets that managers use to decide: designing a workbook with separate input, calculation and output areas, using absolute and relative references and named cells, logical, lookup and summary functions, cleaning imported data, tables, filters, validation, conditional formatting, pivot tables and charts, combining sheets and files, protecting personal data, testing for errors and documenting the work. It is written for supervisors and managers in Jamaican businesses and public bodies.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. A manager who can build a good spreadsheet can track a budget, forecast sales, work out commission and show a board what is happening, without waiting for someone else. A manager who builds a bad one can mislead the whole organisation. This unit teaches you to build **complex spreadsheets that are correct, clear, safe and easy for others to use**.

The notes use the functions common to Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc. Names of functions are the same in all three; menu names differ a little. Follow the program your Centre uses.
**Who it is for:** supervisors, officers and managers who prepare budgets, sales and staff reports, and who check spreadsheets prepared by others.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Decide the purpose, users, inputs and outputs first, then lay out separate, labelled areas for inputs, calculations and results.
Use relative, absolute and mixed references, named cells, and the right order of operations.
Use logical, lookup and summary functions
Use IF, AND, OR, SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, lookups, IFERROR and ROUND to make the sheet decide and report.
Fix imported data: extra spaces, text stored as numbers, duplicates, dates and leading zeros.
Use tables, sort, filter, validation, conditional formatting, pivot tables and honest charts.
Bring branch or department figures into one summary, and manage the links.
Lock formulas, protect personal data, control versions and treat macros with care.
Test with known figures, trace errors, and leave a notes sheet so others can use and maintain the file.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions on formulas, functions, data and security. Some ask what a formula returns.
A **written paper** with short answers (function names, error values, results of formulas) and longer written answers.
**Group practical tasks** on a Centre computer: a budget-against-actual workbook, and a clean-up and pivot-table analysis of a year of sales data. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: In this unit, the one habit that earns most marks is **testing with figures you already know the answer to**. Work the sum by hand first, then check the sheet.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Do not open the program and start typing. Spend five minutes on the plan. A spreadsheet that grows without a plan becomes hard to check and easy to break.

flow: **Purpose**: what decision will the sheet help someone make?
**Users**: who will enter data, who will read results, and how skilled are they?
**Outputs**: what totals, comparisons, flags and charts are needed?
**Inputs**: what data is needed, from where, how often, in what form?
**Calculations**: what rules join inputs to outputs (for example, variance = actual − budget)?
**Layout** and **controls**: sheets, names, validation, protection, backup

head: Area
What goes there
Good practice
rows: Rates, thresholds, lists (such as departments), and the figures people type in
Label each cell clearly and give key cells a **name**. Mark input cells with one colour, such as light yellow.
The raw records: a list or table, one row per record, one heading per column
No blank rows or columns inside the list. One type of data per column.
Formulas that work on the data
Never type a number into a formula if it can be a labelled cell: no 'hard-coding'.
Results, flags, charts for the manager
Short, clear, printable on one page. Everything here comes from formulas, not typing.
Purpose, inputs, key formulas, owner, version, date
So others can use, check and maintain the file.

blocks.p: Keeping them separate makes the workbook easier to **check, use and update**. If the GCT rate changes, you change one settings cell, not forty formulas.

ul: Give sheets meaningful names ('Budget', 'Actuals', 'Summary'), not 'Sheet1'.
Put headings in the first row, and use **freeze panes** so they stay on screen when you scroll.
Use consistent formats: dates as dates, money with J$ and two decimal places or none, percentages as percentages.
Keep totals at the top or clearly separated, and do not leave unexplained blank cells.

blocks.p: A **named cell or range** is given a label such as USDRate instead of a reference such as $H$1. A formula like =B2*USDRate is easier to read, easier to check, and still points to the right cell when copied. Names must not contain spaces and must not look like a cell reference.

blocks.note: Complex does not mean difficult to follow. If you cannot explain a formula in one sentence, split it into steps in helper columns.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Every formula starts with **=**. It can use cell references (B2), numbers, operators (+ − * / ^) and functions. The program follows the order **brackets, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction**. Use brackets to make your meaning clear.
When you **copy** a formula, the program adjusts the references. This is useful and also the commonest source of error.

head: Type
Looks like
What happens when copied
Use for
rows: Both column and row move with the formula. Copy =B2*C2 down from D2, and D5 holds =B5*C5
Calculations along a row or down a column
Neither moves. The cell stays H1 wherever the formula goes
A single rate, threshold or total, such as the GCT rate
The column stays A, the row changes
Tables where one reference runs across and another down
The row stays 2, the column changes

blocks.p: The **$ sign** is placed before the column letter or row number you want to fix. The shortcut key F4 cycles through the types in most programs.

**Example:** a price list in column B and a rate in H1. If C2 holds =B2*H1 and is copied down, C3 becomes =B3*H2, which points to an empty cell, so the results are wrong. The fix is =B2*$H$1, copied down.

head: Function
What it does
Example
Notes
rows: Adds the numbers in a range
If the cells hold 1,200, 850, 0 and 450, the result is 2,500
Mean of the numbers in a range
**Ignores empty cells and text.** 12, 18, empty, 30, 20 gives 80 ÷ 4 = 20, not 80 ÷ 5. A zero is counted.
Counts cells that are not empty (numbers or text)
Rounds to a set number of decimal places
Round money to two decimals so that shown and stored amounts agree
Count or add only the cells that meet one condition
The condition goes in quotes, with the operator

blocks.note: Rounding in the display (formatting) changes only what you see, not the stored number. If invoice lines are rounded for display but added unrounded, the printed total may be a cent out. Use **ROUND** inside the formula where the cent matters, for example for GCT on invoices.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Percentage of a whole: =part/whole, formatted as a percentage.
Percentage change: =(new−old)/old. If last year's sales are J$800,000 in A2 and this year's J$920,000 in B2, =(B2-A2)/A2 shows 15%.
Variance: =actual−budget; variance %: =variance/budget.
Share of total: =B2/$B$10 (the total cell is absolute).

blocks.note: A cell formatted as a percentage holds the fraction: typing 5% stores 0.05. Do not type 5 and then format it as a percentage, or it becomes 500%.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **IF(test, value if true, value if false)** makes the sheet decide. The test compares things with >, <, >=, <=, = or <>.

head: Need
Formula idea
Example result
rows: Pay 5% of sales as bonus if sales are at least J$50,000, otherwise 0
Show 'High' if A1 is more than three times B1
Sales at least J$1,000,000 and no complaints
Chase if marked late or more than 7 days
Three or more outcomes (**nested IF**, or IFS)

blocks.p: For many bands, a **lookup to a table** of band limits is easier to maintain than a long nested IF, because you change the table rather than the formula.

head: Function
Meaning
Example
rows: Add the values in sum_range where range meets one condition
=SUMIF(A2:A6,"Bar",C2:C6). With Bar, Kitchen, Bar, Rooms, Bar against 1,500, 2,000, 2,500, 3,000, 500 the result is 4,500
Add where **all** conditions are met (note the order: sum range first)
Count the cells that meet one or several conditions
Average of the cells that meet the conditions

blocks.p: A **lookup** finds a value in the first column of a table, such as a product code, and returns a value from the same row, such as a price. The price list should have one **unique code** per row.

head: Function
How it works
Points to watch
rows: Looks down the **first column** of the table and returns from the column number given
**Use FALSE (exact match)** for codes. TRUE (approximate match) can return a wrong price silently. Cannot look to the left. Column number changes if you insert columns.
XLOOKUP(value, lookup range, return range, if not found)
Looks in one range and returns from another; exact match by default; can look left
Newer function: not in very old versions of the program.
MATCH(value, range, 0) finds the row; INDEX returns the value from that row of another column
Works in all versions, looks in any direction, survives inserted columns.

blocks.p: **Example:** =VLOOKUP(A2,Prices!$A$2:$C$200,3,FALSE) looks up the code in A2 in column A of the Prices sheet and returns the third column of that row. The table reference is **absolute** so it does not slip when copied down.

blocks.h: Error values and what they mean

head: Error
Usual cause
Fix
rows: Dividing by zero or by a blank cell (a month with no guests)
A lookup cannot find the value (a new code, a typing error, extra spaces)
Check the code and spaces; add the code to the table
A formula refers to cells that have been deleted
A misspelt function or an unknown name, such as =SUMM(A1:A5)
Wrong type of data, such as text in a calculation
Check for text stored where a number is expected
A formula refers, directly or through others, to its own cell
Rewrite so that the total does not include itself
The column is too narrow for the number or date

blocks.p: **IFERROR(formula, message)** shows a message instead of an error value, for example =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(...),"Code not found"). Use it carefully: a message such as 'Code not found' helps; replacing every error with 0 hides problems and makes totals wrong.

blocks.note: A lookup that returns the wrong answer without an error is more dangerous than one that shows #N/A. Always use exact match for codes and test a few lines by hand.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Data that comes from an accounts system, a till or a CSV file is often untidy. **Clean it before you analyse it**, record each fix, and keep a copy of the original.

head: Problem
Why it matters
Cure
rows: Extra spaces before or after text
'Kitchen ' is not the same as 'Kitchen', so lookups and SUMIF miss it
The pivot table lists them as two branches
Standardise with Find and Replace or a lookup table; then use a drop-down list for new data
Numbers stored as text (left-aligned, green corner mark)
SUM ignores them; sorting is wrong
Convert to number (Text to Columns, VALUE, or multiply by 1)
Dates stored as text, or in a different order (day/month or month/day)
Convert with the date format or DATE function; check a few by eye
Format the column as Text **before** pasting or opening the CSV file
Remove Duplicates, or check by a key such as invoice number; keep the original
Blank rows or merged cells inside a list
Break sorting, filtering and pivot tables
Delete blank rows; avoid merged cells in data

head: Function
Use
Example
rows: Pick out part of a code
Check that every code is the same length

blocks.p: A date is stored as a number of days, so you can calculate with it. If an invoice date is in A2 and customers have 30 days to pay, the **due date** is =A2+30. Days overdue today = **TODAY() minus the due date**, for example =TODAY()-(A2+30), shown only if the answer is above zero: =MAX(0,TODAY()-(A2+30)). Other useful functions are EDATE (add months), EOMONTH (month end), DATEDIF and NETWORKDAYS (working days).

ul: Check the **row count** and the **total value** against the source system.
Check that dates, numbers and leading zeros came in correctly.
Check column headings and that there are no hidden rows.
Keep the raw file unchanged and work on a copy.

blocks.note: Never delete the original import. Keep it on its own sheet and write down every cleaning step in your notes. The assessor and your manager need to see that nothing was lost.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Format a list as a **table** (structured range). Formulas and charts built on a table take in new rows automatically, and headings stay with the data. **Sort** to order records. **Filter** to show only some, for example the Montego Bay branch in March. A filter hides rows, it does not delete them; totals typed with SUM still include hidden rows, while SUBTOTAL ignores filtered rows.

**Data validation** limits what can be typed into a cell: a drop-down list of departments, whole numbers between 1 and 31, dates in this year, or a custom rule. It stops staff typing department names in different ways. Add a clear input message and an error message. Validation does not check data that was pasted over it, so check after pasting.

**Conditional formatting** changes the look of a cell by a rule: turn a line red when the variance is more than 10% over budget, amber when between 5% and 10%, green when within. Rules use the data, so they update automatically. Do not rely on colour alone: add a text flag as well, for people who cannot see the colours and for printouts in black and white.
A **pivot table** summarises a large list without writing formulas: drag 'Branch' to rows, 'Month' to columns and 'Amount' to values to see sales by branch and month in seconds.

head: Feature
Notes
rows: A clean list with one heading per column and no blank rows. Best if formatted as a table.
A pivot table does not update by itself. **Refresh** it after the data changes, and make sure its source range includes the new rows (a table does this).
Group dates by month, quarter or year.
% of total, running total, difference from previous month.
Pivot tables are quick and flexible for exploring. SUMIFS formulas update at once, sit in fixed positions and can be linked to a budget or other calculations.

blocks.h: Charts: choose the type and keep it honest

head: Chart
Best for
Avoid
rows: A trend over time, such as occupancy by month over two years
Comparing groups or categories, such as branches
Shares of a whole, with only a few parts (up to about five)
Many slices, or comparing two pies
Whether two measures are related, such as price and number sold
Columns for amounts and a line for a percentage

ul: Give each chart a **title that states the message**, label the axes and units (J$ thousands), and add a legend only if needed.
Start the vertical axis at **zero** for columns and bars, or the chart exaggerates small changes.
Use one colour scheme, and colours that people with colour-blindness can tell apart.
One message per chart; put no more than two or three charts on a dashboard.

blocks.p: **Freeze panes** keeps headings on screen. To print a wide sheet, set **print titles** (repeat heading rows on every page), **fit to one page wide**, choose landscape, and set a print area.

sections.title: Combining sheets and files; protecting and sharing

ul: **Another sheet in the same workbook:** =Kingston!F20 takes cell F20 from the sheet named Kingston.
**Adding the same cell across sheets:** =SUM(Kingston:Portmore!F20) adds F20 on every sheet between the two (a 3-D reference).
**Another file (external link):** formulas contain the file name and path. They break or show old data if files are moved, renamed or opened without updating.

blocks.p: To combine several branches, give every branch **the same template**: same cost lines in the same rows, same headings, layout locked. Then the summary can add them cell by cell. Add a **check cell**: the sum of the branch totals must equal the summary total.

blocks.note: Double counting is the commonest consolidation error: adding a branch's total row as well as its individual lines, or including the same branch twice. Compare the summary total with a total worked on a calculator.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: To let branch heads enter figures but not change formulas: **unlock the input cells, then protect the sheet** (with a password if needed). Locked is the default for all cells, and it only takes effect when the sheet is protected.

A workbook holding staff salaries, bank details or customers' phone numbers contains **personal data**. The general aims of the **data protection law** are to collect only what is needed, use it only for its purpose, keep it accurate and secure, and keep it no longer than necessary.

ul: Remove columns that are not needed (for example, bank details in a report for managers).
Store the file in a **secure folder** with limited access, and set a **strong file password**.
Do not e-mail it or copy it to a personal phone or flash drive.
Share a summary without names where possible.
Delete it securely when the retention policy says it is no longer needed.

blocks.note: Hiding a column or sheet is not security: anyone can unhide it. Protect the whole file with access controls and a password.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Keep one **master file** in a shared, backed-up location.
Use a clear file name: Budget_2026-27_v03_2026-11-07.
Keep a **version log** on the notes sheet: date, who, what changed.
Agree who may edit which area; use sharing features that track changes, and do not circulate copies by e-mail.

blocks.p: A **macro** is a set of recorded steps that can be replayed, for example formatting a monthly report in one click. Benefits: saves time, same steps every time. Risks: errors repeated faster, hard to maintain if no one understands it, and **macro-enabled files can carry harmful code**. Open only macro files from trusted sources, never turn on macros in an unknown file, and document what each macro does.

blocks.h: When to move beyond a spreadsheet

blocks.p: A spreadsheet is cheap and flexible. But when many staff update one large file, versions multiply, there is no audit trail, data is duplicated and errors increase. That is the time to consider a **database or business system** with controlled access and records of who changed what.

flow: Check the design against the purpose
Enter **test data with known answers** (including zero, blank, large and missing items) and compare
Check totals **cross-cast**: the sum of the row totals must equal the sum of the column totals
Compare totals and row counts with the source system
Ask someone else to try to break it
Record the tests and sign off before using it for real

head: Tool or check
What it does
rows: Shows the cells that feed a formula, useful for a total that looks wrong
Shows which formulas use a cell
See the formulas rather than results; step through a long formula
Flags inconsistent formulas, numbers stored as text and circular references
Does the result make sense? Is it close to last month? Is a percentage between 0 and 100?
Row counts and control totals match the accounts system

blocks.p: Add a **notes sheet** with the purpose, inputs and sources, key formulas explained, assumptions, limits, the owner and the version log. So others can use, check and maintain it, and so that your work does not depend on your memory.

A company pays 3% commission on monthly sales up to J$1,000,000 and 5% on the whole amount if sales are above J$1,000,000, but only if there are no unresolved complaints. Put the threshold (F1), the lower rate (F2) and the higher rate (F3) in labelled cells. With sales in B2 and complaints in C2:

Test: sales J$800,000 with no complaints gives 800,000 × 3% = J$24,000. Sales J$1,200,000 with no complaints gives 1,200,000 × 5% = J$60,000. Sales J$1,200,000 with a complaint gives 0. Always test the boundary: exactly J$1,000,000 gives 3%, because 'above' means more than.

Long hours at a screen cause neck, back, eye and wrist problems. Set the screen at **eye level**, sit well supported with feet flat, keep wrists straight, take short breaks every 30 to 60 minutes, and look away from the screen. Learn keyboard shortcuts to reduce mouse strain.

blocks.note: A spreadsheet is only as good as its inputs and checks. A wrong figure that looks professional is more dangerous than an untidy sheet that is right.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: plan a workbook by purpose, users, inputs, calculations and outputs
keep inputs, data, calculations and results in separate, labelled areas and name key cells
write formulas using the correct order of operations
use relative, absolute and mixed references and say what a copied formula becomes
use SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, COUNTA and ROUND and work out their results by hand
use IF, AND, OR and nested IF for decisions, with test cases
use SUMIF(S), COUNTIF(S) and lookups with exact match, and explain common lookup mistakes
name common error values and fix them, and use IFERROR sensibly
clean imported data: spaces, text numbers, duplicates, dates and leading zeros
use tables, sorting, filters, data validation and conditional formatting
build and refresh a pivot table and choose an honest chart
combine branch sheets or files and manage the risks of links
protect formulas and personal data and control versions
test a workbook with known answers, trace errors and document it on a notes sheet

terms: Workbook / worksheet
The file; one sheet inside it.
Cell reference
The address of a cell, such as B2.
Relative / absolute / mixed reference
A reference that moves when copied; one fixed with $; one with only the column or row fixed.
Named range
A label given to a cell or range, used in place of its reference.
Function
A built-in calculation such as SUM or IF.
Nested IF
An IF placed inside another IF to give more than two outcomes.
Lookup
A function that finds a value in a table and returns related data.
Exact match
A lookup that accepts only an identical value (FALSE or 0).
Data validation
Rules that limit what can be entered in a cell.
Conditional formatting
Formatting that changes automatically by a rule.
Pivot table
A tool for summarising a list by groups without writing formulas.
Circular reference
A formula that refers to its own cell.
Trace precedents
A tool that shows which cells feed a formula.
Macro
A recorded set of steps that can be replayed.
Cross-cast
Checking that row totals and column totals give the same grand total.
Hard-coding
Typing a fixed number into a formula instead of using a labelled cell.

c1.title: Treasure Beach guest house
c1.text: Mrs Sandra Willis runs a guest house in Treasure Beach with 8 rooms. Her workbook has a settings sheet and a data sheet. Each row of the data sheet gives a room type in column A, nights sold in column B, the nightly rate in column C and revenue in column D (=B*C). The GCT rate is kept in cell G1. In September (30 days) the guest house sold 168 room-nights in total. Some rows of the data sheet were typed with a space after the room type.

c2.title: Hardware store price list
c2.text: A hardware store in Savanna-la-Mar keeps a price list on one sheet: column A holds the product description, column B the price and column C the product code. Order lines are typed on another sheet, where staff enter the code in column A. The owner, Mr Wayne Brissett, wants the unit price to appear automatically in column B and the line value in column C. Some items were added to the list last week and a few order lines now show errors.

c3.title: Regional sales summary
c3.text: A distributor has three branch sheets in one workbook: Portmore, Mandeville and Black River. Each sheet has monthly sales by product line in rows 3 to 12 and the branch total in row 13. The finance officer, Ms Tracy-Ann Powell, builds a summary sheet to give the company total. She also receives the budget from a separate file kept on a shared drive. Branch heads must enter their own sales figures but must not be able to change any formula.

c4.title: Commission workbook
c4.text: The sales manager of a car parts firm builds a workbook to work out monthly commission. The rule: 4% is paid on the part of a salesperson's monthly sales above J$900,000, but only if there are no unresolved complaints. The threshold is in F1 and the rate in F2. Sales are in column B and complaints in column C. The workbook lists 25 sales staff with their names, TRN numbers and salaries, and several managers have asked for a copy. The manager records a macro to format the monthly report.

c5.title: Till export and monthly analysis
c5.text: A supermarket in Half Way Tree exports each month's sales as a CSV file from its till system. The analyst, Kerry-Ann Mills, opens it and notices that product codes beginning with 0 have lost their zero, some dates look odd, and the export shows 5,320 data rows while the till system reports 5,326 transactions. She builds a pivot table of sales by department and week, and later adds new rows to the data but the pivot table still shows the old totals. She then charts weekly sales for a presentation.

questions.q: In column E, Mrs Willis wants the GCT on each line, using the rate in G1. Which formula in E2, copied down, gives the right result on every row?
o: =D2*G1, which is typed once and then copied to every row in the column to save time
=D$2*$G$1, which fixes the row of the revenue figure and the position of the rate cell
=D2*$G1, which fixes the column of the rate and lets the row follow the revenue figure
questions.why: $G$1 stays fixed when the formula is copied, while D2 changes to D3, D4 and so on. The other versions either move the rate cell or fix the wrong part of the revenue reference.

questions.q: SUMIF is used to total revenue for 'Deluxe' rooms, but the answer is lower than expected. Which is the most likely cause, and the best fix?
o: Some cells hold 'Deluxe ' with a trailing space; clean them with TRIM
The SUMIF range is too long, so it should be shortened to the first few rows
The nightly rates are formatted as text, so the revenue column should be re-typed
The room type is in capital letters, so the formula needs to use UPPER first
questions.why: A trailing space makes 'Deluxe ' a different text from 'Deluxe', so SUMIF skips those rows. TRIM removes extra spaces. SUMIF is not case-sensitive.

questions.q: What was the occupancy rate in September, and how is it worked out?
o: 21%: 168 room-nights sold divided by 8 rooms, then shown as a percentage of the month
5.6%: 168 room-nights sold divided by 30 days, then divided by the 8 rooms again
56%: 168 room-nights sold divided by 300 room-nights, using 10 days as the planning period
70%: 168 room-nights sold divided by 240 room-nights available (8 rooms × 30 days)
questions.why: Occupancy = room-nights sold ÷ room-nights available. 8 × 30 = 240, and 168 ÷ 240 = 0.70, or 70%. Check: 70% of 240 = 168.

questions.q: Mrs Willis wants any room type with revenue under J$150,000 to show 'Review' in column F and nothing otherwise. Which formula is correct?
o: =IF(D2>150000,"Review",""), which shows the message when revenue is above the limit
=IF(D2<150000,"Review"), which leaves out the value used when the test is not met
=IF(D2=150000,"Review",""), which shows the message only when revenue is exactly that figure
questions.why: IF(test, value if true, value if false). The test must be 'less than', and the empty text "" stands for 'nothing'. The other forms test the wrong condition or leave out part of the formula.

questions.q: Mr Brissett wants the price in column B of the order sheet to come from the price list using the code typed in column A. The code column of the list is to the right of the price column. Which approach works?
o: VLOOKUP with the column number set to 1, because the price column is the first column of the list
VLOOKUP with a negative column number, which tells the program to look back along the row
XLOOKUP, or INDEX with MATCH, because they can return a value from a column to the left of the code
A SUMIF on the code column, which will return the matching price without a lookup
questions.why: VLOOKUP searches only the first column of its table and returns from the right, so it cannot return a price that sits to the left of the code. XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH can look in any direction.

questions.q: Several order lines show #N/A after new items were added to the price list. What should Mr Brissett check first?
o: Whether the price column has been formatted as currency, since text prices can stop a lookup
Whether the codes typed on those lines exist in the list exactly as typed, with no extra spaces
Whether the order sheet has been protected, since a protected sheet cannot return values
Whether the list has been sorted in ascending order of description
questions.why: #N/A means the lookup did not find the value. Codes typed with a mistake or a space, or items missing from the list, are the usual causes. Sorting matters only for approximate match.

questions.q: One lookup column uses the last argument TRUE (approximate match). Some lines show prices for the wrong product, with no error. What should he do?
o: Change to exact match (FALSE, or 0 in MATCH) for product codes and test some lines by hand
Leave it, because approximate match is faster and an error would show if it were wrong
Wrap the formula in IFERROR so that any wrong price is replaced by zero
Sort the order lines by code so the approximate match can find them in order
questions.why: Approximate match returns the nearest smaller value when the code is not found, so wrong prices appear without any warning. Exact match shows #N/A for a missing code, which is the safe result.

questions.q: The owner wants a clear message instead of #N/A on an order line when a code is not in the list. Which formula idea is best?
o: IFERROR around the lookup, returning 0 so the total of the order still adds up
Delete the line from the order sheet until the code has been added to the list
Format the cell so that error values are shown in white text on a white background
IFERROR around the lookup, returning the text 'Code not found' so the line is noticed
questions.why: A clear message makes the problem visible and the line can be corrected. Returning 0 or hiding the error makes the order total wrong and the mistake easy to miss.

questions.q: Ms Powell's summary needs the Portmore total from cell F13 of the Portmore sheet. Which formula is correct?
o: =F13!Portmore
=Portmore.F13 typed in the summary cell
='F13'Portmore, with the cell reference placed first
=Portmore!F13
questions.why: A reference to a cell on another sheet puts the sheet name, an exclamation mark and the cell address: SheetName!Cell. The other forms are not valid references.

questions.q: The summary total is far larger than the company's real sales. Ms Powell used =SUM(Portmore!F3:F13)+SUM(Mandeville!F3:F13)+SUM(BlackRiver!F3:F13). What is the likely error?
o: The sheet names should have been written in capital letters, so that the program can recognise them
SUM cannot add cells on different sheets, so the answer has been estimated by the program
Each range includes row 13, the branch total, as well as its lines, so sales are counted twice
The three formulas should have been typed as text and joined, so that the program adds them in the right order
questions.why: Rows 3 to 12 hold the lines and row 13 already adds them, so including row 13 double counts. Compare the summary with a total worked on a calculator, and use a check cell.

questions.q: The budget figures come from a separate file on a shared drive, linked into the summary. What is the main risk?
o: The link makes the summary sheet too large to be printed on a single page
If the file is moved or renamed, the link breaks or shows old figures
Links to other files cannot be used in formulas, so the figures will not calculate
A linked file is always opened in read-only mode so that nobody can correct or update the budget
questions.why: External links hold the file name and path. If the file moves or is renamed the link breaks, and if it is not updated the summary may show out-of-date figures. Document the sources and check them each month.

questions.q: How can Ms Powell let branch heads type in their sales but stop them changing formulas?
o: Unlock the input cells, then protect the sheet
Hide the formula rows and the columns so that branch heads cannot see them
Protect the sheet first and then unlock the input cells afterwards in a new file
Save the workbook as a PDF and ask each branch head to type into the PDF
questions.why: Cells are locked by default, but locking works only when the sheet is protected. Unlock the cells people may edit, then protect the sheet. Hidden rows can be unhidden and a PDF cannot update the workbook.

questions.q: Which formula in D2 correctly works out the commission for the rule in the case, using F1 and F2?
o: =IF(C2=0,B2*$F$2,0), which pays 4% of the whole sales figure when there are no complaints
=IF(B2>$F$1,B2*$F$2,0), which pays 4% on the whole amount once sales pass the threshold
=IF(C2>0,(B2-$F$1)*$F$2,0), which pays only when there is an unresolved complaint
questions.why: The rate applies only to the amount above the threshold, and only when there are no complaints. MAX(0, ...) stops a negative amount for sales below J$900,000.

questions.q: To test the workbook before use, the manager enters sales of J$1,350,000 with no complaints. What should the commission be, and what does the test show?
o: J$54,000, which is 4% of the whole J$1,350,000 of sales for the month
J$13,500, which is 1% of the sales since the threshold is about two-thirds of the total
J$0, because the sales are too high for the commission rule to apply
J$18,000, which she can check by hand: 450,000 × 4%
questions.why: (1,350,000 − 900,000) × 4% = 450,000 × 0.04 = J$18,000. A test with a known answer shows whether the formula follows the rule; also test sales below the threshold and a case with a complaint.

questions.q: Several managers ask for a copy of the whole workbook. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Send the whole file by e-mail, since managers are trusted and the file has a password
Hide the personal columns before sending the file, so that the data does not need to be removed
Send a version without names, TRN numbers or salaries, or share a protected summary only
Print the whole sheet for each manager, because paper copies cannot be shared or changed by anyone else
questions.why: TRN numbers and salaries are personal data. The general aim of the data protection law is to use only what is needed for the purpose and keep it secure. Hidden columns can be unhidden, so remove the data or restrict access.

questions.q: The manager records a macro to format the monthly report. What should she keep in mind?
o: A macro cannot make mistakes, so it needs no testing once it has been recorded
Document what the macro does and open macro-enabled files only from trusted sources
Macros work only on one computer and cannot be used in a shared file
Macro files are always safe, because the program checks them for harmful code
questions.why: A macro repeats its steps, including mistakes, and macro-enabled files can carry harmful code. Test it, document it and be careful about the source of files with macros.

questions.q: After opening the CSV file, the product codes that begin with 0 have lost the zero. What is the best way to prevent this next month?
o: Add the zero back by hand each time and then check the codes against the till
Format the code column as Text before importing, or import it as text
Use ROUND on the code column so the leading zeros are retained
Change the number format to percentage so that the zeros are displayed
questions.why: Leading zeros are dropped when a column is treated as numbers. Setting the column to Text before import keeps codes as they are. ROUND and percentage formats do not restore them.

questions.q: The export shows 5,320 rows but the till system reports 5,326 transactions. What should Kerry-Ann do?
o: Find out which six transactions are missing before analysing, since totals may be understated
Go ahead with the analysis, because a difference of six rows out of 5,326 is too small to matter
Add six rows of average value to the data so that the count matches the till system
Delete the till system's figure, since the CSV file is the one the pivot table uses
questions.why: Row counts and control totals should match the source. A gap means records are missing, perhaps because the export was cut off, and results may be wrong. Find the cause first.

questions.q: She adds new rows to the data but the pivot table's totals do not change. What should she do?
o: Retype the totals on the pivot table, since the program does not update summaries
Protect the sheet so the pivot table is locked to the correct figures
Sort the data from the oldest to the newest so the pivot table can read it
Refresh the pivot table, and make sure its source range includes the new rows
questions.why: A pivot table does not update automatically. It needs a refresh, and its source range must take in the new rows; formatting the source as a table does this automatically.

questions.q: For the presentation she wants to show how weekly sales changed over twelve weeks. Which chart is best, and what is an honest choice for its vertical axis?
o: A pie chart with twelve slices, starting each slice at the top of the circle
A line chart with the axis starting just below the lowest value, to make the changes easier to see
A line chart, starting the vertical axis at zero or clearly marking any break
A scatter chart of week against department, with no labels so that it looks cleaner
questions.why: A line chart shows a trend over time. Starting the axis at zero (or marking a break) avoids exaggerating small changes. A pie shows shares of a whole, not change over time.
